extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning how to write and read mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing, structuring, and justifying elementary undergraduate-level mathematical proofs (logic, set theory, number theory, epsilon–delta limits, relations). Emphasizes proof strategies, translating logical forms, and common conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving a number is composite (not prime)
rubrics_metrics.description: To say that an integer larger than 1 is not prime means that it can be written as a product of two smaller positive integers (∃a ∈ Z+∃b ∈ Z+(ab = n ∧ a < n ∧ b < n)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the goal is to prove 'n is not prime', exhibit explicit positive integer witnesses a and b and prove the three component facts (ab = n, a < n, b < n). This is an existential proof: introduce witnesses and verify their properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential-instantiation in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a hypothesis asserts an existential statement, the proof may apply existential instantiation to introduce the witnessing objects into the proof (e.g., from 'n is not prime' introduce a and b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After introducing witnesses, the remainder of the proof is devoted to showing they satisfy the required properties. The proof need not explain how the witnesses were discovered (scratch work is omitted); it must only demonstrate they work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure for proving conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the remaining goal is a conjunction (e.g., x y = 2n − 1 ∧ x < 2n − 1 ∧ y < 2n − 1), treat it as several separate subgoals and prove them one at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose conjunctions into independent targets and handle with elementary algebra or separate arguments; make each subproof explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of algebraic cancellation and pattern recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Long algebraic products may simplify by cancellation so that complicated expressions reduce to the desired result; such simplifications often motivate choices of witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although '…' or pattern shorthand may be used informally, be aware that this hides a pattern-dependent argument; a fully rigorous justification (for example via induction) should be provided when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction for negative statements or 'there are infinitely many...'
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative statements (like 'there are infinitely many primes', which is logically ¬(finitely many primes)) are often proven by contradiction: assume the negation (finitely many primes) and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate the negated claim into a precise existential or universal form (e.g., 'there exists n such that there are n primes' and a list p1,...,pn). Apply existential instantiation to introduce those objects and construct a counterexample (e.g., m = p1·...·pn + 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases for disjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a key fact about an object is a disjunction (e.g., m is either prime or a product of primes), it naturally suggests proof by cases: handle each possibility and show the desired conclusion follows in both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly label cases when helpful and in each case derive the existential or contradiction desired. Even if not labeled in final write-up, recognize the structure is conditional on cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing counterexamples via product-plus-one trick
rubrics_metrics.description: In arguments about primes, form m = p1·p2·...·pn + 1 to produce a number that is not divisible by any listed primes, forcing either a new prime factor or a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show m is not divisible by any pi by computing remainders; then apply the 'either prime or product of primes' dichotomy to reach contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing explicit sequences to avoid primes
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce n consecutive composite integers, choose x = (n+1)! + 2 so that for each 0 ≤ i ≤ n−1, x+i is divisible by i+2 and hence composite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write each x+i as (i+2)·(something smaller) to show compositeness. Verifying a few early terms may be redundant but can improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding unnecessary verifications for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes specific verifications (e.g., checking x and x+1 separately before the general case) are unnecessary for correctness but are included to make the proof easier to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such extra checks are stylistic choices; include them if they aid comprehension, but recognize they aren't required for the logical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon–delta proof structure (limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a limit statement lim_{x→c} f(x) = L: let ε>0 be arbitrary, find δ>0 such that for all x, 0<|x−c|<δ implies |f(x)−L|<ε. The final proof lists: let ε be arbitrary, choose δ, let x be arbitrary, assume 0<|x−c|<δ, then prove the inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do scratch work to find a δ that makes |f(x)−L| bounded by ε, but omit scratch steps in final write-up. Work backwards: bound |f(x)−L| by a constant times |x−c| to pick δ = ε/constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing δ by factoring and bounding
rubrics_metrics.description: In many examples you can simplify |f(x)−L| algebraically (e.g., factor numerator to cancel x−c), yielding an expression like k|x−c|, so choosing δ = ε/k suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify algebraic manipulations (e.g., factoring) carefully; justify cancellation by noting x ≠ c under the 0<|x−c| hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scratch work versus final proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Scratch work used to find witnesses (like δ) is not part of the formal proof; the final proof simply states the chosen value and proves it works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should understand the omitted search, but the written proof only needs the justification that the chosen value satisfies the quantified condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set equality: two standard approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two sets equal you can either prove ∀p[p ∈ A ↔ p ∈ B] or prove both inclusions A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A (i.e., prove two subset relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-inclusion method is often preferred; each inclusion is handled by letting an arbitrary element of one set be given and showing it belongs to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-chasing proofs using arbitrary elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving subset or membership claims, introduce an arbitrary element p of the source set and deduce properties to show p belongs to the target set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When p is known to be an ordered pair, it is customary to write p = (x,y) and existentially instantiate coordinates immediately to simplify reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppressing explicit ordered-pair introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is clear an arbitrary element of a Cartesian product must be an ordered pair, mathematicians often directly denote it as (x,y) rather than first proving it equals some (x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conventional suppression is acceptable when clarity is maintained; for teaching, the book sometimes shows the explicit step first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving subset relations involving unions via case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When given (x,y) ∈ (A×B) ∪ (C×D), use proof by cases: either (x,y) ∈ A×B or (x,y) ∈ C×D, handle each case to show (x,y) ∈ (A∪C)×(B∪D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the cases and in each derive the required membership; this follows the standard pattern for subset proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving A×∅ = ∅ via contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A×∅ = ∅, assume contrary that A×∅ ≠ ∅, so ∃p(p ∈ A×∅). Introduce p = (x,y) and derive contradiction because y ∈ ∅ is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize equality to the empty set is a negative statement; proof by contradiction is a natural strategy, using existential instantiation to produce impossible elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful treatment of edge cases (empty set) in informal reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal plausible arguments can fail when sets might be empty. For example, attempting to prove A=B from A×B = B×A by picking a coordinate y∈B fails if B=∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check and handle edge cases such as emptiness explicitly; if necessary, break the proof into cases that consider empty sets separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving iff statements by separate directions
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'iff' statement should be proven by establishing both the forward and backward implications separately, often using different strategies (e.g., assume nonemptiness to get elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For disjunctive conclusions (A=∅ ∨ B=∅ ∨ A=B), use proof by cases; for negated disjunctions use De Morgan to work with positive assumptions (A≠∅ ∧ B≠∅) and then existentially instantiate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer positive statements over negative ones when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative statements (like A=∅) are often awkward in proofs; negating them to obtain positive existential assumptions (A≠∅ → ∃x∈A) can be more useful for constructing arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use De Morgan's laws to convert compound negatives into positive conjunctive assumptions that enable the introduction of concrete elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and reasoning about relations (domain, range, inverse, composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard definitions: Dom(R) = {a ∈ A | ∃b ∈ B((a,b) ∈ R)}; Ran(R) = {b ∈ B | ∃a ∈ A((a,b) ∈ R)}; R^{-1} = {(b,a) ∈ B×A | (a,b) ∈ R}; S ∘ R = {(a,c) ∈ A×C | ∃b ∈ B((a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning about relations, apply these definitions directly; ensure the middle set matches when composing relations, and use existential instantiation to witness domain/range membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating informal English statements into precise logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the logical form of claims (e.g., 'sequence of n consecutive integers containing no primes' is ∀n>0∃x>0∀i(0 ≤ i ≤ n−1 → x+i is not prime)), and plan proofs according to quantifier order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match proof strategy to logical form: to prove ∀n∃x∀i P, let n be arbitrary, construct x (existential), then let i be arbitrary and prove P( i ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing when a proof uses standard proof strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the overall proof method from the logical structure (existential introduction, proof by contradiction, proof by cases, direct proof with arbitrary element, induction for pattern-dependent algebraic manipulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the chosen strategy explicitly when helpful; use the rules for each strategy (e.g., existential instantiation, assumptions for contradiction, case assumptions for disjunction).
